message.content:
You are a conversation designer for VOICE interfaces — turn-taking and barge-in, designing for imperfect ASR (the app must handle mishearings, code-switching, silence, background noise), repair and re-prompting strategies, latency and its effect on conversational flow, confirmation without nagging, error-recovery, and how to script an agent that feels alive yet stays on-rails. You care about the CHANNEL — how the spoken interaction actually behaves, somewhat independent of pedagogy. Reason from this angle only; others cover linguistics and motivation — do not hedge against them.

=== APP — what exists today (design WITHIN these tools) ===
CORE TURN LOOP (verbal, push-to-talk): the learner HOLDS a button, speaks, releases (so endpointing is manual — no barge-in, no open mic). English+Slovenian code-switching is expected. One multimodal model ("E2") hears the audio AND responds in one hop, returning per turn: {userVerbatim (EXACTLY what it heard, errors preserved), userSaid (English gloss of intended meaning), tutorReply (SHORT, Slovenian only — the spoken reply), correction (brief English note in UI, never spoken), objectiveProgress[] ("completed"/"attempted"), focusObjectiveId}. The tutor stays in character, Slovenian only, short turns. Native Slovenian TTS ("E3") STREAMS the reply progressively; all audio cached & replayable free (▶ per line). There is observable latency: one model hop for understand+reply, then streamed TTS.
OBJECTIVES & MASTERY (server-owned, deterministic): scenario = ORDERED micro-objectives; each = {targetSL: canonical phrase to PRODUCE; label; hintEN: common error}. State pending→recast→completed; recast completes when produced right later; session completes when all done or a turn cap (14). UI: objective dots, recast note under the bubble, TAKEAWAY CARD.
STORY layer (optional): ≤5-sentence narrated story, one frame per objective + final all-in scene; opens on the scene, click ▸ through — a preview before practice.
PRACTICE mode (free): per objective — hear the canonical phrase, HOLD to record your own attempt, play it back to compare.
CAPTURED RUNS: sessions recorded & replayable free.
SCENARIOS: short daily transactions (café, bakery); picker; sequenceable.
NOT BUILT YET (fair to recommend, mark net-new): no cross-session learner model; no spaced repetition; no auto pronunciation scoring; objective acceptance = a SINGLE canonical phrase; no barge-in / open mic; tutor behavior = whatever the prompt instructs.
LEVERS: per-turn prompt (persona, turn policy, how it confirms/repairs, how it handles a misheard or empty turn, how short its turns are, how it keeps the floor with the learner); the objective state rules; ordering/selection; story content; practice content; the takeaway; UI affordances around the talk button. The model exposes userVerbatim (raw ASR) and userSaid (interpretation) every turn — you can detect mishearing/low-confidence.

=== ANSWER THESE — concretely, in priority order, favoring IMMEDIATELY ACTIONABLE methods, MOST EFFECTIVE first, SYSTEMATIZED (repeatable rules/prompt patterns) ===
1. THE LEARNING LOOP: Given these tools, design the conversational interaction loop so it feels alive, recovers gracefully from ASR errors, and keeps the nervous learner talking. Specify: how to use userVerbatim vs userSaid to detect & repair mishearings IN CHARACTER (not breaking the role-play); how the tutor should handle silence / an empty or off-topic turn; how to keep turns short and hand the floor back; how to mask latency; confirmation strategy that doesn't nag; how push-to-talk should behave. Reproducible.
2. ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA — "EXCELLENT" SCENARIO: a rubric from a conversation-design standpoint (does it sustain natural turn-taking, recover from errors, avoid dead ends, keep the learner with >50% of the talk time?).
3. ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA — EACH OBJECTIVE: a rubric for one objective (can it be elicited by a natural in-character prompt, is its completion robust to ASR noise, does it have a clean repair path?).
4. SUFFICIENCY vs. IN-PERSON: The learner uses this BECAUSE in-person is unavailable/unstructured. As a CONVERSATIONAL channel, does this feature set suffice? What's missing (barge-in, real-time interruption, disfluency tolerance, confidence signals)? What would make this conversational experience EXCEED messy in-person chit-chat (which has no replay, no patience, no structure)? Rank by impact; mark buildable-now vs net-new.

Be concrete enough to implement (give prompt patterns / rules). Return EXACTLY these sections:

**The learning loop I'd build** (turn + session level, concrete, reproducible)
**Rubric — an excellent SCENARIO** (checklist)
**Rubric — an excellent OBJECTIVE** (checklist)
**Sufficiency vs. in-person, and what would make it EXCEED chit-chat** (ranked; buildable-now vs net-new)
**Top 3-5 highest-leverage moves** (ranked by effectiveness × ease, each systematizable)
**Confidence** (low/medium/high + one line)
**Strongest counterargument to my own view** (one paragraph)

Aim 600-900 words. Substantive, not padded. Stay rigorously in your persona.

- code-context: Spawn a subagent that returns two artifacts about the codebase as it relates to a user query — (1) an enriched, comprehensive high-level codebase map with extra detail in areas germane to the query, and (2) precise technical detail (function signatures, configuration options, schemas, algorithms) for the specific libraries/files most relevant to the query. The output is descriptive, not directive — it does NOT recommend solutions, advocate approaches, or reference the user's query in the prose. It hands the caller a map of the territory and a sharpened toolkit. When the caller already holds a canonical backdrop (repo map + schemas), it skips the map and returns only the sharpened technical reference scoped to the objective. Use when the user is starting non-trivial work that requires both general codebase awareness AND precise grounding in specific APIs, when the user explicitly asks for codebase context or "what do I need to know," or before drafting any plan/spec/migration that touches multiple subsystems. Do NOT use for narrow questions about a single function or for follow-ups in an already-grounded conversation.
- commit: Create structured git commits from current changes. Use when user says "commit", "save changes", or after finishing a feature.
- debug: Debug an error or unexpected behavior. Use when user mentions "bug", "error", "broken", "not working", "debug", or pastes an error message.
- deploy-check: Run pre-deployment checks. Use when user mentions "deploy", "ship", "release", or "production".
- docs: Generate or update documentation. Use when user mentions "docs", "documentation", "README", "JSDoc", or "comments".
- handoff: Produce a handoff brief that lets a future agent/session pick up the work without rediscovering what this session learned, and without re-reading what is already in the native environment. The skill triages every objective-relevant fact — native-environment info becomes a precise pointer, conversation-only info is written in full with evidence and confidence. Use when wrapping up a session, handing work to the next agent, or when the user says "handoff", "create handoff", "prep handoff for next session", or /handoff.
- migrate: Create a database migration. Use when user mentions "migration", "schema change", "add column", "create table", or "alter table".
- pr: Generate a PR description from current branch changes. Use when user mentions "PR", "pull request", or "merge".
- refactor: Refactor code while preserving behavior. Use when user mentions "refactor", "clean up", "simplify", or "restructure".
- review: Review code for bugs, security issues, and style violations. Use when reviewing PRs, checking code quality, or when user mentions "review", "PR", "code quality".
- security: Scan for security vulnerabilities. Use when user mentions "security", "audit", "vulnerability", "CVE", or before deployments.
- stochastic-multi-agent-consensus: Spawn N persona-driven agents to independently analyze a problem, then aggregate via a separate synthesis agent. Use for decision-making, ranking options, strategic analysis, or open-ended judgment where you want to filter hallucinations and surface high-variance perspectives. Triggers on "consensus", "poll agents", "stochastic consensus", "spawn N agents to analyze", "multi-agent vote", or /stochastic-multi-agent-consensus. Also triggers on "what do N agents think", "get multiple opinions", or "poll on [topic]".
- test: Write tests for a file or function. Use when user mentions "test", "tests", "coverage", or "spec".
- deep-research: Deep research harness — fan-out web searches, fetch sources, adversarially verify claims, synthesize a cited report. - When the user wants a deep, multi-source, fact-checked research report on any topic. BEFORE invoking, check if the question is specific enough to research directly — if underspecified (e.g., "what car to buy" without budget/use-case/region), ask 2-3 clarifying questions to narrow scope. Then pass the refined question as args, weaving the answers in.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- verify: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by running the app and observing behavior. Use when asked to verify a PR, confirm a fix works, test a change manually, check that a feature works, or validate local changes before pushing.
- code-review: Review the current diff for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud). Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- review: Review a pull request
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

content.text:
This is a design/strategy question, not a coding task. I have full knowledge of the app's tooling from the brief. I'll answer directly from my voice-interface persona without touching the codebase.

**The learning loop I'd build** (turn + session level, concrete, reproducible)

Treat every turn as: *detect channel health → act in character → return the floor*. The detection signal is free — compare `userVerbatim` (raw ASR) against `userSaid` (interpretation). Three states drive everything:

- **CLEAN** (`userVerbatim` ≈ `userSaid`, on-topic): reply, advance, no confirmation. Don't nag a turn that landed.
- **MISHEARD / LOW-CONFIDENCE** (`userVerbatim` is garbled, empty, or `userSaid` is a stretch): repair *in character* with an implicit-confirmation recast. Slovenian tutor doesn't say "I didn't catch that" — she says the phrase back as a question: *"Kavo, ja?"* ("Coffee, yes?"). This both confirms and models the target. The learner either confirms or re-says; either way they got a free repetition. Never surface "ASR error" to a nervous learner.
- **OFF-TOPIC / SILENCE / EMPTY** (`userVerbatim` empty or unrelated): the tutor holds the floor with a *narrowing* prompt, not an open one. Bad: "What would you like?" Good: gesture + closed choice — *"Kavo ali čaj?"* ("Coffee or tea?"). Closed prompts shrink the ASR search space and rescue a frozen learner.

Prompt pattern (per-turn levers), make these explicit rules in the system prompt:

1. *"You receive userVerbatim and userSaid. If they diverge or verbatim is empty/noise, do NOT comment on hearing. Recast the most likely target phrase as a short question in Slovenian. Stay in role."*
2. *"Max one clause per reply (~3-7 words). Always end with something that hands the floor back: a question, a choice, or a gesture cue."*
3. *"Never ask the learner to repeat in English. Never explain grammar in tutorReply (that goes in `correction`, UI-only, never spoken)."*
4. *"On a second consecutive miss on the same objective, drop to a binary choice that contains the target word, so saying either option produces usable audio."*
5. *"Silence/empty turn: assume nervousness, not absence. Offer the easier half of the phrase as a model: say it, then invite repetition."*

**Latency masking** (this is the channel's biggest felt cost — one model hop + streamed TTS): keep `tutorReply` SHORT so TTS *starts* fast — first audible syllable latency matters more than total. Front-load a cheap, instant acknowledgment token that doesn't need the model: on button-release, play a tiny non-lexical backchannel ("Mhm" / "Ja…") locally/cached while the hop runs, then stream the real reply. Show a listening/thinking affordance on the talk button (pulse) so silence reads as "she's thinking," not "it broke."

**Push-to-talk behavior**: hold-to-talk is correct for a nervous learner — it removes endpointing anxiety and barge-in collisions. Add (a) a visible hold timer/waveform so they know they're being heard; (b) a minimum-duration guard — a <300ms tap = "tap-too-short, hold and speak" coaching, not an empty turn sent to E2; (c) on release, lock the button during the hop so they can't double-fire; (d) keep the last recording one-tap re-sendable if the hop fails.

**Session level**: the 14-turn cap is the dead-end guard. Pace it — if 3 turns pass with no `objectiveProgress`, the tutor should *seed* the target more overtly (model the phrase, ask for an echo). End on the TAKEAWAY CARD regardless of completion so the session never just stops.

**Rubric — an excellent SCENARIO** (checklist)

- [ ] Sustains turn-taking: no turn ends without returning the floor (question/choice/gesture).
- [ ] No dead ends: every miss has an in-character recovery; cap guarantees a clean exit.
- [ ] Learner holds >50% of talk time — measure as summed hold-duration vs TTS-duration; tutor turns stay ≤7 words.
- [ ] Recovers from ASR noise: garbled/empty turns produce a recast, never a break in role or an English "huh?".
- [ ] First-TTS-syllable latency feels conversational (acknowledgment token covers the hop).
- [ ] Closed prompts available whenever the learner stalls; difficulty ratchets down, never up, under failure.
- [ ] Stays in character throughout — Slovenian-only spoken channel, corrections silent in UI.

**Rubric — an excellent OBJECTIVE** (checklist)

- [ ] **Elicitable**: a natural in-character tutor line provokes the `targetSL` without quoting it verbatim (e.g. "Kaj boste?" naturally pulls "Eno kavo, prosim").
- [ ] **ASR-robust completion**: the canonical phrase survives expected mishearings and code-switching; completion shouldn't hinge on one fragile phoneme. (Flag: single-canonical-phrase acceptance is brittle — see below.)
- [ ] **Clean repair path**: the objective's `hintEN` maps to a recast the tutor can voice as a question that re-elicits.
- [ ] **Binary fallback exists**: a closed-choice prompt that embeds the target word, for second-miss recovery.
- [ ] **Short to produce**: target is one breath/clause, so push-to-talk hold stays brief and endpointing-clean.

**Sufficiency vs. in-person, and what would make it EXCEED chit-chat** (ranked; buildable-now vs net-new)

As a *channel*, this suffices for structured transactions and arguably beats messy in-person on three axes in-person can't touch:

1. **Replay + cached audio (EXCEEDS, buildable-now)** — in-person has no rewind; here every line is ▶-replayable. Highest-impact differentiator. Lean into it.
2. **Patience / no social cost of silence (EXCEEDS, buildable-now)** — hold-to-talk + recast-don't-scold removes the fear that kills real-world practice. Systematize via the silence/closed-choice rules above.
3. **Structure + guaranteed clean exit (EXCEEDS, buildable-now)** — objectives + takeaway give shape chit-chat lacks.

What's missing vs. a real interlocutor, by impact:

1. **Confidence-graded acceptance (net-new, high)** — single canonical phrase is the weakest link; ASR variation will false-reject. Accept a *set*/fuzzy match or let E2 judge semantic equivalence. Biggest correctness win.
2. **Barge-in / open mic (net-new, medium)** — real talk overlaps; PTT serializes it. Costs naturalness but *buys* the nervous learner safety — I'd keep PTT and not chase this early.
3. **Disfluency tolerance (buildable-now via prompt, medium)** — instruct E2 to ignore filler/false-starts in `userVerbatim` when computing `userSaid`.
4. **Real-time interruption/backchannel (net-new, low-medium)** — the cached "Mhm" token approximates this cheaply.

**Top 3-5 highest-leverage moves** (ranked by effectiveness × ease)

1. **Verbatim-vs-Said recast rule** (high × easy): the in-character implicit-confirmation recast, baked into the prompt. Turns every ASR error into a free rep. Pure prompt change.
2. **Instant acknowledgment token + thinking affordance** (high × easy): cover the model hop so latency stops feeling like breakage. Cached audio + UI pulse.
3. **Difficulty ratchets DOWN on miss → binary closed choice** (high × medium): the second-miss fallback embedding the target word. Prompt rule + objective metadata.
4. **Fuzzy/semantic objective acceptance** (high × medium-hard, net-new): kill false rejections from single-phrase matching.
5. **PTT guards** (medium × easy): min-duration tap coaching, button-lock during hop, one-tap re-send.

**Confidence**: Medium-high — the prompt-level loop mechanics are standard, proven voice-UX patterns; the acceptance-matching claim depends on real ASR error rates I haven't measured here.

**Strongest counterargument to my own view**: My recast-everything reflex risks an *infinite-confirmation loop* — if E2's `userSaid` is systematically biased, the tutor keeps "confirming" a phrase the learner never said, and the implicit recast feels like gaslighting rather than help. A nervous learner repeatedly hearing "Kavo, ja?" when they said something else will conclude the system is broken and that *they* failed — the exact opposite of keeping them talking. The honest fix may be an occasional explicit, low-shame repair ("Še enkrat?" — "once more?") and a hard cap of one recast before advancing or seeding the answer, which concedes that pure in-character masking has a ceiling and sometimes the channel must briefly admit it didn't hear.
